hook: Dell founded the company that became Dell Technologies in January 1984 and has led it since, most recently as Chairman and CEO. Dell has become a principal supplier of the servers used for AI training and inference, with the company reporting a record $95 billion AI server backlog in its fiscal second quarter 2027 results announced September 1, 2026.
name: Michael Dell

quote.text: AI is the operating model of the modern enterprise.
quote.context: Michael Dell, keynote address at Dell Technologies World 2026, quoted on the Dell Technologies blog, May 18, 2026

moniker: Founder, Chairman and CEO of Dell Technologies

reading.body:
Dell Technologies held a $95 billion backlog of AI server orders as of September 2026, making it a critical chokepoint in the hardware supply chain that constrains AI scaling.

The backlog reflects demand that outpaces Dell's ability to deliver. In fiscal Q2 2027, the company shipped $16.4 billion in AI server revenue while taking $60.9 billion in new orders. This gap between inflow and outflow is the operating reality of compute scarcity. Dell did not reach this position by accident. Michael Dell founded the company in 1984 and has led it continuously, building organizational capacity to serve enterprise infrastructure over four decades. That existing operation became the vessel into which AI demand poured.

The data covers Dell's order book and revenue, not the underlying constraints on fulfilling it. A backlog this size could reflect demand exceeding manufacturing capacity, supply chain delays in components, or both. It does not show whether Dell or its suppliers control the binding constraint, or whether that constraint is components, assembly labor, facility space, or power availability for data centers receiving the servers. The backlog is a symptom of scarcity, not a diagnosis of its cause.

For AI scaling, this matters because servers must exist before compute exists, compute must exist before capability exists, and Dell's delivery timeline now shapes how fast enterprises can train and run models. A company cannot scale AI infrastructure faster than its hardware suppliers can build it.
